name: Privacy for Students With Disabilities
title: Privacy for Students With Disabilities
answer: Privacy for students with disabilities means treating evaluation results, diagnoses and behavior records as among the most sensitive information a school holds, and keeping identifying details away from any AI tool that is not covered by a signed data privacy agreement. It matters because careless sharing can follow a student for years, and because trust between families and schools is hard to build and easy to lose.

sections.body: This idea sets a stricter standard for the special education data that passes through AI tools than for ordinary school information. Evaluation results, diagnoses and behavior records are described as among the most sensitive data a school holds, and they can trail a student for years when they are shared without care. The problem it solves is the quiet spread of identifying details into tools that were never reviewed or agreed to. The rule is that every AI tool touching special education data must sit under a signed data privacy agreement, and tools without one should never see identifying information about a student with a disability. Alongside that rule sits a habit, which is removing names and other identifying details before asking a tool for help.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In day to day use, the name removal habit carries most of the weight. A teacher seeking help with a goal or a behavior plan describes the need in general terms, leaving out names, birth dates, school names and rare details that could point to one student. The text notes that in a small school even a combination of grade and disability can be enough to identify a single child, so the guidance is to leave a detail out when there is any doubt. Before a tool is used at all, staff check that it is covered by a signed data privacy agreement, and tools that are not covered are kept away from identifying information. The text does not set out separate steps by grade band, so the same habit applies wherever a student's special education information is involved.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no study, figure or evidence label for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. What it provides instead is a standard drawn from the sensitivity of the data and from the consequences of careless sharing, namely that records can follow a student for years. It also points to the fragility of family trust as a reason for care, describing that trust as hard to build and easy to lose. No findings are cited to show how often identifying details leak or what harm follows, and none should be assumed.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are firm in the text. A tool that is not covered by a signed data privacy agreement should never see identifying information about a student with a disability, and the name removal habit applies even when a tool is covered. The judgement calls stay with people, including deciding whether a combination of grade and disability could identify a child in a small school and deciding what counts as a rare detail. Families should be told which tools handle their child's special education information, through a short list shared at the annual IEP meeting that explains what each tool does and how the district protects the data. Families who ask questions deserve clear answers, and that conversation remains a human responsibility rather than something delegated to a tool.
